title: Which AI to use for what
intro: There are five names you're going to hear all the time: ChatGPT, Claude, Claude Code, Gemini, and Copilot. Here you'll see what each is good at, where it's weak, what it costs per month, and which one to open depending on what you want to do. By the end you'll have your pair of tools picked out and you'll know when to switch from one to the other.

theory.title: They all do almost the same thing, until they don't
theory.text: Behind all five is the same core idea: a model, meaning a giant program that has read a huge amount of text and, when you write something to it, keeps predicting what word comes next. That's why all five can summarize an email, write you an ad, or explain why you're getting an error. Most of what you'll ask for, any of them can do, and you won't notice the difference. The differences show up in everything else: very long texts, multi-hour tasks, up-to-the-minute information, and actually touching real files. Choosing well means knowing where each one breaks down, not which one is the best overall.
theory.analogy: It's like five gas-powered cars. They'll all get you to the supermarket. The difference shows up when you have to climb a mountain pass with a full trunk.

theory.title: The three things they actually differ on
theory.text: First: how much text they can hold in mind at once, called the context window. If you paste in a 60-page contract, one reads the whole thing and another only keeps the beginning and fills in the rest by guesswork. Second: what it's connected to. Gemini lives inside Google and can look at your Gmail or your Drive if you let it; ChatGPT searches the internet very well; Claude sticks more to its own reasoning but thinks more carefully with what you give it. Third, and the one that will matter most to you: whether it only answers you or also does things on its own — creating files, changing them, building you a website and testing it. That last one is what separates talking about your idea from having your idea done.
theory.analogy: One gives you the recipe; another gives you the recipe, opens the fridge, turns on the stove, and cooks it for you. Both know how to cook. Only one gets you dinner.

theory.title: The five in one sentence, warts included
theory.text: ChatGPT is the all-rounder: it writes well, searches the internet, understands photos, talks by voice, and has the most polished app; in exchange it can get wordy, and its best models are behind the paid plan. Claude is the one that writes the most natural English and hallucinates the least when you give it a long document; in exchange it searches the internet worse and cuts you off sooner on the free plan. Claude Code is Claude turned into a handyman: it takes your project's whole folder and creates, changes, and tests the files on its own; in exchange it's operated by typing commands into a black window called a terminal, and that's not for your first day. Gemini is unbeatable if your life is in Google and it handles very long documents and videos; in exchange it falls short on long, well-polished answers. Copilot lives inside the program where code is written and predicts your lines as you type, and it's the cheapest one; in exchange, if you don't write code yet, it's useless to you.
theory.analogy: ChatGPT is the Swiss army knife, Claude the good pen, Claude Code the handyman with a van, Gemini the one who has the keys to your house, and Copilot an excellent screwdriver: useless if there's no screw.

theory.title: What it's going to cost you per month
theory.text: The four that run in a browser all have a genuine free plan, with a daily message cap that's plenty to get started. The paid plans all land in the same range, between $20 and $25 a month: ChatGPT Plus around $23, Claude Pro around $20 (a bit less if you pay for the whole year), Google AI Pro around $22 including 2 TB of storage. Copilot is the cheap one: about $10 a month or about $100 a year, and it's free if you're a student and verify your school. Claude Code isn't billed separately — it's included in Claude Pro; if you used it daily there are higher tiers from $90 to $200 a month. There are also max plans of $200 to $275 a month that you don't need anywhere close to. These prices shift every few months and are almost always advertised without tax, so mentally add your local rate.
theory.analogy: Think of it like gym memberships: paying for two at once is throwing away $45 a month. Pay for one, use it to the fullest, and lean on free for the rest.

theory.title: If you want to do X, use Y
theory.text: Write a long text that sounds like a person, not a brochure? Claude. Search for something that happened this week, with links? ChatGPT or Gemini. Summarize a 200-page PDF or a two-hour video? Gemini. Understand a contract or a report without it inventing clauses? Claude. Make an image or edit a photo? ChatGPT or Gemini. Talk by voice while you drive? ChatGPT or Gemini on your phone. Get the data from twenty invoices into a table? Gemini if they're in your Drive, ChatGPT if you upload them by hand. Have it build you a website, a calculator, or a demo that looks and works? Claude, and if the project grows, Claude Code. Work on an entire folder of files for hours without forgetting anything? Claude Code, once you get there. Autocomplete code as you type in your editor? Copilot. Dig through your Gmail and your calendar? Gemini, and nobody else.
theory.analogy: No useful question starts with 'which one is best'. They all start with 'what do I want to do right now'.

theory.title: The rule of two
theory.text: Pay for one subscription and keep another one open for free. The paid one is for the long haul, the one that builds your thing. The free one is your second opinion: when the first gets stuck, acts dumb, or gives you an answer that smells off, you paste the same thing into the other and compare in thirty seconds. Switching tools mid-task doesn't break anything; the only thing you lose is the thread of the conversation, so copy the last good message before you jump. And don't get married to any of them: the one that was ahead six months ago might be second today and pull ahead again next month.
theory.analogy: Like having two doctors: a primary care one and another for a second opinion when the diagnosis doesn't sit right.

tasks.title: Open all three free ones and ask them the same question
tasks.action: Open three tabs: chatgpt.com, claude.ai, and gemini.google.com. On each, the sign-up button is in the top right (says Sign up or Get started). Register with your email. None of the three asks for a card for the free plan: if it does, you've landed on the paid plan by accident — go back. Once you're in, paste the same text into all three text boxes and hit Enter.
tasks.prompt: I want to do this: [describe your idea in two or three sentences, the way you'd tell a friend at a bar]. I've never coded. Explain what parts this breaks down into, which is the hardest, and where you'd start. No jargon: translate every unusual word in parentheses.
tasks.expect: Three different answers to the same question, one per tab. They'll agree on substance and differ in tone and detail. Notice which one you understood best: that clue is worth more than twenty comparison articles.
tasks.stuck: If Gemini sends you to your Google account, use the same one you already have on your phone. If Claude asks for a phone number to verify you, that's normal and only happens once.

tasks.title: Give them the same long task and see which one holds up
tasks.where: In the three tabs you already have open
tasks.action: Now a real task, one you'll actually notice. Paste this text into all three and read all three answers in full. Don't look for which one is correct: look for which one you'd copy and paste without touching anything.
tasks.prompt: Write me the homepage for [your project]: a headline, three sentences explaining what it is and who it's for, and six frequently asked questions with their answers. Plain, natural English, second person, no brochure words like solutions, innovative, or synergy. Make it sound like one person explaining it to another.
tasks.expect: Three full texts. Almost always one clearly sounds more human and the other two smell like an ad. Note which one it was: that's your go-to for anything involving writing.
tasks.stuck: If one gives you something short or generic, it's because you didn't give it enough context. Add two more sentences about who it's aimed at and ask again.

tasks.title: Turn on slow-thinking mode
tasks.action: All of them have a short gear and a long gear. The short one answers instantly; the long one stops to reason and gets things with logic, numbers, or chained steps far more right. In ChatGPT, the selector is at the very top where the model name shows: pick the one that mentions Thinking or reasoning. In Claude, next to the text box there's a button to ask it to think longer before answering. Turn it on and paste the prompt.
tasks.prompt: I have $300 total to get my idea off the ground. Think it through carefully before answering. Give me an exact breakdown of that $300 across the things that actually need paying for, tell me what can be done for free, and warn me where I'm likely to get overcharged. Figures in dollars, annualized.
tasks.expect: Before the answer you'll see a notice that it's thinking, and it takes anywhere from ten seconds to a minute instead of answering instantly. The answer comes with numbers that add up, not a generic list.
tasks.stuck: If you can't find the button, start your message with: think this through step by step before responding. It works almost as well.

tasks.title: Upload a document of yours and compare the summaries
tasks.action: Find a PDF you have lying around that you don't mind sharing: a manual, some terms, a report. The longer, the better. In all three text boxes there's a paperclip or a plus-sign button on the left: click it, pick the file, and wait for its name to show up. Then paste the prompt. Warning: whatever you upload travels to that company's servers, so nothing like payslips, medical reports, or other people's data.
tasks.prompt: Read the whole document. Tell me in five bullet points what it says, then three specific things in it that someone would easily miss. Cite the page for each one. If something isn't in the document, tell me it's not there instead of assuming it.
tasks.expect: A summary that mentions real data and real pages from the file. If you pick a random page and ask what's on it, it should tell you what's actually there. Gemini tends to be the one that handles very long documents best.
tasks.stuck: If it says the file is too large, upload just the chapter you're interested in, or ask the AI itself how to split it.

tasks.title: Ask for something you can see working, not something described to you
tasks.action: This is the difference that's going to change your day the most. Open a new conversation in claude.ai and paste the prompt. Don't touch anything else: nothing to install, no other program to open.
tasks.prompt: Build me a simple calculator for my business: I enter a product's price, what it costs me, and how many units I sell a month, and it tells me the monthly and yearly profit. Make it look nice, in English, and have it work right here so I can try it.
tasks.expect: A panel opens on the right with the calculator built and working: you type numbers and get results. That's an artifact, an actual thing rather than text describing it. Try asking make the colors green and add sales tax, and watch it update itself.
tasks.stuck: If it responds with a wall of text and symbols inside a gray box instead of opening the panel, tell it: don't give me the code, build me the app so I can use it right here.

tasks.title: Deliberately hit the free limit
tasks.action: It's worth knowing where your ceiling is before it catches you mid-task on something important. Keep going in the calculator conversation and ask for ten or fifteen changes in a row without stopping: change colors, add fields, ask it to explain things. At some point it will stop you.
tasks.expect: A message warning you that you've hit the limit and when you'll be able to write again, usually in a few hours. Note roughly how many messages it let you send: that number is what you'd be buying the day you pay.
tasks.stuck: If you don't hit the limit, good for you: it means the free plan gives you plenty of room for now. Try it again the day you start a long project.

tasks.title: Try Copilot without installing anything and rule out what doesn't apply to you
tasks.action: Go to github.com/copilot. It'll ask for a GitHub account, which is free. You'll see a chat similar to the others. Write it the prompt and compare with what you've already seen.
tasks.prompt: Explain, no jargon, what you do that ChatGPT or Claude don't, and at what point in someone's learning journey — for someone who's never coded — would you actually start being useful to them.
tasks.expect: It answers well, but you can tell it wants you to show it a code project so it can shine. The takeaway: Copilot helps once you're already writing code in an editor, and today it isn't your tool. You just saved yourself $10 a month and an afternoon of installation.
tasks.stuck: If it asks you to choose a repository (a project folder saved on GitHub) and you don't know what that is, close the tab. You don't need anything from there yet.

tasks.title: Find out if Claude Code is for you yet or not yet
tasks.action: In the left-hand menu of claude.ai, check whether something called Code shows up. Open it if it's there and read the welcome screen without installing anything. Claude Code is the same Claude, but working on an entire folder on your computer: it creates files, changes them, tests them, and fixes what it breaks, all in a row, without you having to walk it through every step.
tasks.expect: Either you see the option and understand what it's about, or you don't see it and know it exists for later. Both outcomes are fine. If it starts talking about installing something or typing commands in a black window called a terminal, close it and leave it: that comes in its own guide, once your project is big enough.
tasks.stuck: If you want a clear rule: switch to Claude Code the day you have more than ten files and you're sick of copying and pasting between the web and your computer. Not before that.

tasks.title: Get Gemini searching through your own stuff
tasks.where: In gemini.google.com, with your Google account
tasks.action: This is the one thing no one else does. Type the prompt below into Gemini. A Google window may pop up asking for permission to access your Drive or your Gmail: read it before accepting, because you're giving it access to your email. If you'd rather not, skip this task, no problem, you're not missing anything from the rest.
tasks.prompt: Search my Drive for the three most recent documents related to [your topic] and give me a one-line summary of each, telling me the exact file name.
tasks.expect: Real names of your own files, not made up. If it gives you names that don't exist, it hasn't actually accessed anything: try again or check the permissions you gave it.
tasks.stuck: To revoke its access afterward: go into your Google account, connected apps section, and remove the permission. It can be undone anytime.

tasks.title: Build your own decision card
tasks.where: In whichever AI you liked best
tasks.action: You've now seen all five from the inside. Now have it build you a cheat sheet tailored to you. Paste the prompt, swapping the list for the things you actually do every week.
tasks.prompt: These are the five things I do every week: [1], [2], [3], [4], [5]. For each one, tell me which to use among ChatGPT, Claude, Claude Code, Gemini, and Copilot, one sentence of why, and what my backup would be if the first choice gets stuck. As a table, no hedging.
tasks.expect: A five-row table with specific names and specific reasons. Copy it into your phone's notes or a document. When you're not sure what to open, check the cheat sheet instead of losing twenty minutes deciding.
tasks.stuck: If it answers 'it depends' or puts all five in every row, tell it: pick just one per row even if you might be wrong, I need a decision, not options.

tasks.title: Decide what you're paying for and set a reminder before you pay
tasks.where: In your calendar and, afterward, on the chosen AI's website
tasks.action: Pick a single subscription, the one for the long haul, and stick with it for a month. Before you enter your card, open your phone's calendar and set a reminder for three days before the month is up with the text: is what I'm paying for [name] actually paying off? After that, go to that AI's website, hit Upgrade, and choose the monthly plan, not the annual one. Warning: these subscriptions renew automatically each month and the month already charged isn't refunded; canceling takes two clicks from your profile and you keep the plan until the paid period ends.
tasks.expect: The reminder set in your calendar and, if you paid, the plan name visible next to your name inside the app (says Plus, Pro, or similar). And a decision made once and for all, instead of three subscriptions open just in case.
tasks.stuck: If you're torn between two, stay on free for one more month. Paid plans don't expire or go up in price for waiting, and in a month you'll have noticed which one you actually open more.

canDo: Decide in five seconds which AI to open for whatever's in front of you, without reading one more review
Work entirely on free plans until a real project asks for more
Know exactly how much you'll pay per month and what you get for that money
Ask for things that you can see and use, like a calculator or a page, instead of text describing them
Get Gemini to pull data from your own documents and emails, which is the one thing the others don't do
Switch tools mid-task when one gets stuck, without losing what you've already done
cantDo: Trust these prices as if they were fixed: they shift every few months and here they're listed without tax
Expect the one that writes best to also be the one that searches the internet best: they almost never match
Get any value out of Copilot if you don't write code in an editor yet
Start with Claude Code today: it requires installing things and working in the terminal, and that comes later
Trust an answer just because it sounds confident: they invent facts with the exact same confident tone
Upload other people's data, payslips, or medical reports: that ends up on servers that aren't yours
words: The brain behind it: a giant program that has read a huge amount of text and, when you write to it, keeps predicting which word fits next. ChatGPT or Claude are the app; the model is what's inside.
How much text it can hold in mind at once, counting what you've written and what it's replied. When it fills up, it starts forgetting the start of the conversation.
The chunk the AI splits words into to count them, roughly three per every four words. It matters because it's the unit you're billed on when you pay per use instead of by subscription.

When it invents a fact, a law, a quote, or a link and tells it to you with total confidence. It's not lying: it's filling the gap with whatever sounds right. That's why anything involving figures, dates, or proper names gets checked.
The panel that opens next to the conversation with something built and working: a page, a calculator, a document. Claude calls it an artifact and ChatGPT calls it a canvas.
A usually-black window where you type commands to the computer instead of clicking buttons. You don't need it for anything in this guide. It shows up once you get to Claude Code.
The cap on how many messages you can send in a stretch or in a day. On free plans it's low and resets on its own after a few hours. Paying is, above all, buying a higher ceiling.

An AI that, besides answering you, does things on its own: opens files, changes them, checks whether they work, and fixes them. Claude Code is the clear example. The more it does on its own, the more it matters to review what it did.
